audits.basis: No passage of Quataert 1997 was retrievable by any public route this round, so the note-45 report of 1725/1726/1727 remains neither confirmed nor refuted and the claim stays unresolved. What the round did establish: three independent catalog records converge on the registered work identity 'Clothing Laws, State, and Society in the Ottoman Empire, 1720-1829' (IJMES 1997, DOI 10.1017/S0020743800064837), consistent with the prior ledger's identification of the cited study, and all three register it as closed with no open-access location (Unpaywall is_oa false/oa_status closed; OpenAlex best_oa_location null; Semantic Scholar openAccessPdf status CLOSED with publisher-elided abstract). The prior ledger's access verdict (403/paywall on JSTOR and Cambridge Core) is corroborated and extended: the DOI landing served HTTP 429 this session, and the Wayback CDX index holds zero captures of jstor.org/stable/pdf/164587*, so no public archived copy sits at the previously blocked route. Entry bytes at this baseline (sha256 cc1370c937a25ee361ec099bbe10edd2f854c697057813933bcaa5a567e620c1) keep the L118 caution and the L119 (to-verify-from-the-dated-instrument) markers unchanged; no erratum is warranted by catalog metadata, which is not unread contents and is not treated as note-45 confirmation.
audits.coupling_implication: The dress/regulation-date coupling stays open exactly as the entry frames it: a 1720s women's outer-dress regulation is attested in the entry's frame but its precise issuing year is contest-reported, and the conflicting 1725/1726/1727 dates attributed to Quataert note 45 remain unretrievable. Consequence for the corpus: the decree may support 'intended distinctions and an authority's intervention' (entry table L125) but cannot anchor any specific year; any fiction or lesson must keep the date range, never a silently chosen single year, and the L119 dimensions/penalties fields stay (to-verify) from the dated instrument.
audits.limits: The article is closed access per all three catalog APIs and no public full text was found: HathiTrust full-text search, CORE, Mojeek and Ecosia returned HTTP 403; DuckDuckGo served a captcha wall; scholar.archive.org served a session-verification wall on both attempts; SearX and Marginalia returned no usable results; Bing served geo-mangled irrelevant results; fatcat.wiki timed out; archive.org metadata search had zero hits for 'clothing laws' + Quataert; the domain-wide Cambridge CDX query timed out (504), so absence of an archived Cambridge PDF capture is not itself established. Catalogue metadata (title, DOI, journal, year, OA status) was retrieved; the article's page range (403-425), notes and the note-45 contents were not, and remain known only as reported by the prior ledger. Search-engine non-results are recorded as tool failures, not as evidence about the literature.

audits.basis: The lexical half of the coupling is strengthened by a new directly retrieved record: Polish nożyce 'scissors' is inherited from Proto-Slavic *nožici from *nòžь (Wiktionary entry citing PAN and PWN dictionaries), which lands on the corpus label's form almost exactly and matches the prior audit's Slovak nožnice / Russian ножницы (from нож) results; a deity, priesthood or robe reading of the label still has no lexical support, and the implement reading is now supported at the Proto-Slavic level. The contextual half remains open and the negative record grew: the only early-modern scholarly edition of the Laurentian chronicle retrievable here (Cross and Sherbowitz-Wetzor 1953) contains no occurrence of nozhnitsy or scissors anywhere in its translated text, apparatus or notes, and never discusses the Rod/rožanicy cult at all, so the label cannot be anchored there; dic.academic.ru (Sreznevsky-derived and other dictionaries) has zero hits for 'ножници'. Nothing retrieved this round attests the form in a Rod/rožanicy, homiletic or dress context, so 'remains unidentified' is neither confirmed as a settled status nor overturned by a contextual attestation, and the whole claim stays unresolved with the entry's prohibitions standing as the safe course. Entry bytes at this baseline (sha256 b3c2ef4a103db9f9f53a22e3e5c437f28ad09be7797f6464b7214cc2c163250d) keep lines 127-128 and table row 134 unchanged; no erratum is warranted.
audits.coupling_implication: Language-myth-dress coupling verdict: language supports only the implement reading (scissors, Proto-Slavic *nožici from *nòžь, per the PAN/PWN-cited record plus the prior round's Slovak/Russian records); myth (deity or priesthood) has zero lexical or textual support in anything retrieved; dress (garment, embroidery program, color code or Rod/rožanicy-specific ritual costume) has zero support, and the sole early chronicle edition retrievable here is silent on the cult entirely. For the corpus this means costume-table row 134 stays exactly as designed: 'Scissors initiate a kinship rite' remains a proposed ritual action requiring verified term, language, text, place and date, never recovered Slavic fact, and no scissors-bearing birth or kinship costume may be backfilled from the lexical coincidence alone.
audits.limits: The SAV Slovníkový portál (the Slovak kodifikační source behind the Wiktionary nožnice record) serves a bot-check ('Previerka') to non-browser agents, so the Slovak kodification remains Wiktionary-mediated and not directly fetched, unchanged from the prior audit; Google Books API returned HTTP 429 on all attempts, scholar.archive.org a session-verification wall and fatcat.wiki a timeout, so book-level searches for the label in Rod/rožanicy or homiletic contexts could not be run; the absences recorded (1953 edition full text, dic.academic.ru) are negative searches over the sources actually retrievable, not proof that no source attests the label in a ritual-dress context; Ivanits 1989 remains lending-blocked and unrechecked; crowd-edited dictionaries support the lexicon only, not the ritual context.
